items.stem: A patient has a globally stiff, painful shoulder. Which passive movement, when most restricted, is the strongest sign pointing toward frozen shoulder?
options: Passive external rotation
Passive internal rotation
Passive flexion
Passive horizontal adduction
items.explanation: Frozen shoulder follows a capsular pattern: external rotation is proportionally the most restricted movement, then abduction, then internal rotation. Marked loss of passive ER with a firm capsular end-feel — in a shoulder with normal X-rays — is the closest thing to a diagnostic sign the condition has.
items.pearl: No special test diagnoses frozen shoulder. The passive ROM pattern IS the test.

items.stem: The drop arm sign has sensitivity ~27% and specificity ~88–92% for full-thickness rotator cuff tears. What does this profile mean clinically?
options: A positive test substantially raises the probability of a full-thickness tear
A negative test rules out a full-thickness tear
The test is useless because sensitivity is low
It should be used to screen all shoulder patients
items.explanation: High specificity means few false positives — so a POSITIVE result rules the diagnosis in (SpPin). Low sensitivity means many tears are missed, so a negative drop arm tells you very little. Low-sensitivity/high-specificity tests are confirmers, not screeners.

items.stem: A patient reports shoulder night pain. Which feature would make the night pain genuinely concerning rather than routine?
options: Pain when lying on the affected shoulder
Unremitting pain regardless of position, with weight loss
Pain that wakes them when they roll over
Morning stiffness lasting 10 minutes
items.explanation: Night pain is present in most painful shoulder conditions and is a poor discriminator on its own. The concerning pattern is constant, position-independent pain — especially with systemic features (weight loss, fever, night sweats, cancer history). Positional night pain that eases with repositioning is mechanically driven and common in RCRSP and frozen shoulder.
items.pearl: Night pain isn't a red flag. UNREMITTING night pain is.

items.stem: Which comorbidity most increases the risk of frozen shoulder — and should be asked about in every stiff-shoulder history?
options: Diabetes mellitus
Hypertension
Asthma
Osteoporosis
items.explanation: Diabetes raises frozen shoulder risk roughly 5-fold (prevalence ~10–20% in diabetic populations vs 2–5% general), with more severe and treatment-resistant courses. Thyroid disease is the other classic association. A stiff shoulder in a 45–60 year old should always trigger the diabetes question.

items.stem: For rotator cuff related shoulder pain, what does current evidence support as first-line management?
options: Progressive loaded exercise over ≥12 weeks
Early subacromial decompression surgery
Complete rest until pain-free
Routine corticosteroid injection at diagnosis
items.explanation: Trials (including CSAW and comparable exercise trials) show progressive exercise matches surgical decompression at 6–12 months, and decompression performs no better than placebo surgery. Injections can give short-term relief but don't change long-term outcomes. Rest deconditions the cuff — graded loading is the treatment.

items.stem: Why is early ultrasound/MRI often unhelpful in atraumatic shoulder pain?
options: Rotator cuff abnormalities are common in pain-free people, so findings may not explain symptoms
Imaging cannot visualize the rotator cuff
MRI is contraindicated in shoulder conditions
Ultrasound has no role in the shoulder
items.explanation: Cuff tears are found in roughly 20–25% of asymptomatic adults overall, exceeding 50% by the 7th–8th decade. An imaging 'abnormality' in an atraumatic presentation may be an incidental finding — treating the scan instead of the patient drives overdiagnosis and unnecessary surgery. Image when there's trauma, red flags, or failure to progress with good rehab.
items.pearl: Scan findings without a matching clinical picture are noise, not diagnosis.
items.citation: UNVERIFIED — prototype draft; citation pending clinical review

items.stem: A patient cannot hold their arm in external rotation when you place it there — it drifts back to neutral (positive external rotation lag sign). What does this most suggest?
options: Full-thickness tear of supraspinatus/infraspinatus
Subacromial bursitis
Frozen shoulder
Biceps tendinopathy
items.explanation: Lag signs test whether the cuff can HOLD a position, which requires structural continuity. The ER lag sign has specificity ~94–98% for full-thickness posterosuperior cuff tears — a true lag is one of the most convincing bedside findings in the shoulder. Pain-related weakness gives way gradually; a lag drops.

items.stem: Which combination should make you think of a Pancoast (superior sulcus lung) tumor presenting as 'shoulder pain'?
options: Shoulder/medial scapular pain + hand intrinsic wasting + drooping eyelid in a smoker
Painful arc + weak empty can test
Clicking with overhead movement in a swimmer
Morning stiffness that eases in 15 minutes
items.explanation: Pancoast tumors invade the C8–T1 roots and stellate ganglion: shoulder/scapular pain, intrinsic hand weakness/wasting, and Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). Smoking history is the biggest risk factor. These patients see MSK clinicians first because the presenting complaint is 'shoulder pain' — and the shoulder exam is often normal.
items.pearl: A normal shoulder exam in a patient with severe shoulder pain is itself a finding.

items.stem: Your patient's Hawkins-Kennedy is painful. Given these numbers, what's the best conclusion?
options: Small probability shift only — a positive barely changes my differential
Confirms subacromial impingement definitively
Rules out cervical referral
Indicates a full-thickness cuff tear
items.explanation: With specificity 56%, nearly half of people WITHOUT subacromial pathology also test positive. LR+ of 1.8 shifts probability only slightly. Hawkins-Kennedy earns its keep as a rule-OUT test when negative (decent sensitivity), not as a confirmer. No single 'impingement' test can rule the diagnosis in.

items.stem: Spurling's test reproduces your patient's arm pain. Best conclusion?
options: Substantially increases the probability of cervical radiculopathy
Meaningless — sensitivity is too low to use the test at all
Confirms the shoulder itself is the source
Rules out cervical myelopathy
items.explanation: Specificity 93% and LR+ ~7 mean a positive Spurling's produces a large probability shift toward cervical radiculopathy. The low sensitivity means a NEGATIVE test can't exclude it — but that's not what's being asked. Know which direction each test is allowed to push you.
items.pearl: Spurling's: positive is informative, negative is not. The mirror image of Hawkins-Kennedy.

items.stem: You suspect a full-thickness cuff tear, but the drop arm test is negative. Best conclusion?
options: Tear is still very much possible — this test misses most tears
Full-thickness tear is now excluded
The patient has frozen shoulder instead
Sensitivity of 27% means the test was performed incorrectly
items.explanation: Sensitivity 27% means the drop arm misses ~3 of 4 full-thickness tears — LR− of 0.83 barely moves the needle. A negative result should not reassure you. If suspicion is real, use higher-sensitivity findings (ER lag, weakness in ER, age >60) or image.

items.stem: A 63-year-old with sudden weakness after a fall shows a clear external rotation lag. Pre-test probability of a full-thickness tear was ~40%. Best conclusion?
options: Probability now well above 80% — discuss imaging and surgical opinion pathways
Probability roughly unchanged
The lag proves the tear is only partial-thickness
Start with 12 weeks of exercise before telling anyone
items.explanation: LR+ ~7 applied to a 40% pre-test probability pushes post-test probability above 80%. An acute traumatic full-thickness tear in this age group is one of the few shoulder presentations where early imaging and timely surgical opinion genuinely change outcomes — repairs done early do better than late.
items.pearl: Traumatic + weak + lag sign = don't sit on it for 12 weeks.
items.citation: UNVERIFIED — prototype draft; citation pending clinical review

items.stem: Hawkins-Kennedy, painful arc, and infraspinatus resistance are ALL positive in a 48-year-old with atraumatic shoulder pain. Why is this cluster more useful than any single test?
options: Combining tests trades sensitivity for specificity — 3/3 positive gives LR+ ~10, a large shift
Three tests triple the sensitivity
Clusters remove the need for a history
It proves surgery is indicated
items.explanation: Individually these tests have LR+ below 2. Requiring all three positive drops sensitivity but pushes specificity to ~90% (LR+ ~10). Clustering is how weak tests become useful — you accept missing some cases in exchange for confidence when the full pattern is present.

items.stem: A 22-year-old overhead athlete gets apprehension (not just pain) at 90° abduction + external rotation, relieved by a posteriorly-directed relocation force. Best conclusion?
options: Anterior instability is now the leading diagnosis
This confirms rotator cuff tendinopathy
Apprehension is a normal response in athletes
The relocation manoeuvre invalidates the test
items.explanation: When the endpoint is APPREHENSION (guarding, 'it's going to come out') rather than pain, specificity reaches ~90%+, and relief with relocation strengthens it further. Pain as the endpoint ruins the test's accuracy. In a young athlete this pattern makes instability the working diagnosis.
items.pearl: Apprehension tests: the patient's face is the outcome measure, not their pain report.

items.stem: 45-year-old painter. 3 months of gradual lateral shoulder pain, worse with overhead work, painful arc 70–110°, FULL passive ROM including external rotation. No neck pain, no trauma. Rank the differentials, most likely first.
items.explanation: Gradual onset + overhead aggravation + painful arc + FULL passive ROM is the RCRSP signature. Full passive ER effectively removes frozen shoulder from contention. ACJ pathology stays above frozen shoulder (it's overhead-aggravated, though pain is usually superior and end-range). No neck pain or arm symptoms puts cervical referral last — but it stays on the list until screened.

items.stem: 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes. 4 months of progressive shoulder pain, now marked stiffness. Passive external rotation is 50% lost versus the other side with a firm end-feel. X-ray normal. Rank the differentials.
items.explanation: Age 40–60 + diabetes + progressive pain-then-stiffness + major passive ER loss is textbook frozen shoulder. GH osteoarthritis produces the same capsular pattern — which is exactly why the normal X-ray matters (frozen shoulder is a NORMAL-X-ray diagnosis). RCRSP doesn't restrict passive ROM. Cuff tears cause weakness, not capsular stiffness.
items.pearl: Frozen shoulder and GH OA look identical on exam. The X-ray separates them.

items.stem: 23-year-old rugby player. Two previous 'dead arm' episodes tackling, now vague shoulder pain and doesn't trust the arm overhead. Apprehension positive with relocation relief. Rank the differentials.
items.explanation: Young + collision sport + dead-arm episodes + positive apprehension-relocation = anterior instability until proven otherwise. A Bankart lesion is the usual underlying structural cause, so it ranks right behind (arguably the same problem at different levels of description). Cuff pathology is uncommon as a primary diagnosis at 23. Nothing here points to the ACJ.

items.stem: 61-year-old fell off a ladder 2 weeks ago. Since then: can't actively lift the arm past 60°, but you can passively take it to 160°. Weak, painless-ish external rotation. Rank the differentials.
items.explanation: The key dissociation: passive ROM near-full, active ROM severely limited, with true weakness — that's a structural or neurological failure, not pain inhibition. In a >60-year-old after trauma, full-thickness tear leads. Axillary nerve injury (deltoid wasting, regimental badge sensation) is the important mimic after shoulder trauma/dislocation. Frozen shoulder is excluded by the free passive ROM.
items.pearl: Big active–passive ROM gap + weakness = structure or nerve, not 'tendinopathy'.

items.stem: 38-year-old office worker. Aching shoulder/upper arm pain with pins and needles into the thumb and index finger. Neck extension + rotation reproduces the arm symptoms. Shoulder tests unremarkable. Rank the differentials.
items.explanation: Symptoms distal to the elbow in a dermatomal pattern (thumb/index = C6) + reproduction with neck movement + a quiet shoulder exam moves the problem to the neck. Peripheral entrapment (median/radial) can mimic but doesn't respond to neck position. RCRSP rarely refers below the elbow. TOS is a diagnosis of exclusion.

items.stem: 72-year-old smoker. 6 weeks of progressive deep shoulder pain, constant including at rest and at night, 5 kg unintentional weight loss. Shoulder exam nearly normal. Rank what should top your concern list.
items.explanation: Age >50 + smoking + constant non-mechanical pain + weight loss + a pain-out-of-proportion-to-exam picture is a malignancy pattern until investigated — this patient needs medical referral and imaging, not a rehab plan. PMR is the other systemic consideration at this age (check bilateral symptoms, morning stiffness, ESR/CRP). The mechanical diagnoses rank last because the exam doesn't support them.

items.stem: 58-year-old with 8 weeks of shoulder pain. Select every finding in this history that is a genuine red flag requiring escalation.

findings.text: Unintentional weight loss of 6 kg
findings.note: With age >50, unexplained weight loss is a primary malignancy flag.

findings.text: Past history of breast cancer
findings.note: Prior cancer + new persistent MSK pain = rule out metastasis. Breast, lung, prostate, kidney, thyroid metastasize to bone.

findings.text: Pain when lying on the affected side
findings.note: Positional night pain is mechanically driven and near-universal in painful shoulders.

findings.text: Constant pain unchanged by position or activity
findings.note: Non-mechanical pain behaviour — nothing makes it better or worse — is the pattern that should worry you.

findings.text: Painful arc between 60–120°
findings.note: A classic mechanical RCRSP finding.

findings.text: Stiffness after sitting for an hour
findings.note: Brief inactivity stiffness is common and benign.

items.explanation: Three findings escalate this case: weight loss, cancer history, and non-mechanical constant pain. Any one alone warrants attention; together they mandate referral for investigation before any rehab plan. The mechanical findings (painful arc, positional night pain) are reassuring, not alarming.

items.stem: 49-year-old, shoulder pain worsening rapidly over 4 days. Had a corticosteroid injection 10 days ago. Select the red flags.

findings.text: Recent intra-articular injection
findings.note: Any joint injection or surgery is a portal for infection — essential context.

findings.text: Fever and feeling generally unwell
findings.note: Systemic signs + acute joint pain = septic arthritis until excluded. This is a same-day medical emergency.

findings.text: The joint is hot, swollen, and any movement is severely painful
findings.note: The classic septic joint triad: red/hot, effusion, dramatic pain with any ROM.

findings.text: Pain started gradually over months before the injection
findings.note: The chronic backstory is the original mechanical problem — it's the acute change that signals infection.

findings.text: Aged 49
findings.note: Age alone is not a flag here.

items.explanation: Septic arthritis destroys cartilage within days and has real mortality. Post-injection + fever + hot swollen joint + severe pain on any movement = emergency referral for aspiration, not physiotherapy. The speed of change is the signal: a chronic shoulder that suddenly becomes acutely inflamed has a new problem.
items.pearl: Ask every acute-worsening patient: any injections, surgery, or dental work recently? Any fever?

items.stem: 60-year-old man referred with 'left shoulder pain'. Select the findings that suggest this is not a shoulder problem at all.

findings.text: Pain comes on when climbing stairs and settles with rest
findings.note: Exertional, non-movement-specific pain relieved by rest is an angina pattern.

findings.text: Shoulder movement testing does not reproduce the pain
findings.note: If the symptom can't be mechanically reproduced, question the MSK hypothesis itself.

findings.text: Associated breathlessness and jaw tightness during episodes
findings.note: Classic cardiac companions. This patient needs urgent medical assessment.

findings.text: Pain located over the deltoid region
findings.note: Deltoid-region pain is the standard referral zone for most shoulder pathology — location alone doesn't discriminate.

findings.text: History of doing heavy gardening last month
findings.note: A plausible mechanical trigger — but it doesn't explain the exertional pattern.

items.explanation: The unifying signal: pain linked to cardiovascular exertion, not shoulder movement, plus autonomic companions (breathlessness, jaw pain), plus a shoulder exam that can't reproduce it. Visceral referral hides inside MSK caseloads — the exam that fails to reproduce symptoms is telling you where the problem isn't.

items.stem: 68-year-old woman with 6 weeks of shoulder pain. Select the features suggesting an inflammatory condition (e.g. polymyalgia rheumatica) rather than mechanical shoulder pain.

findings.text: Both shoulders affected, and both hips ache too
findings.note: Bilateral girdle (shoulder + pelvic) involvement is the PMR distribution.

findings.text: Morning stiffness lasting over 45 minutes
findings.note: Prolonged morning stiffness (>45 min) is an inflammatory hallmark; mechanical stiffness eases in minutes.

findings.text: New headache and scalp tenderness
findings.note: PMR's dangerous companion is giant cell arteritis — headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms. GCA threatens sight: same-day referral.

findings.text: Difficulty reaching overhead
findings.note: Non-specific — every shoulder condition limits overhead reach.

findings.text: Pain eased somewhat by ibuprofen
findings.note: NSAID response doesn't discriminate inflammatory from mechanical.

items.explanation: Bilateral girdle pain + prolonged morning stiffness in a >50-year-old should trigger the PMR question and inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) — PMR responds dramatically to low-dose steroids, and missing it means months of futile 'rehab'. The GCA screen (headache, scalp, jaw, vision) is mandatory whenever PMR is suspected.

items.stem: 45-year-old with shoulder discomfort and arm symptoms. Select the neurological findings that require escalation rather than routine MSK care.

findings.text: Progressive painless wasting of the hand muscles
findings.note: Progressive painless weakness/wasting suggests motor neuron disease, syrinx, or tumour — never a routine MSK finding.

findings.text: New clumsiness in BOTH hands and recent balance problems
findings.note: Bilateral hand symptoms + gait change = cervical myelopathy pattern (upper motor neuron). Check Hoffmann's, reflexes, gait.

findings.text: Pins and needles in the thumb when the neck is extended
findings.note: Position-dependent dermatomal paraesthesia fits cervical radiculopathy — manage as MSK, monitor for progression.

findings.text: A single episode of arm tingling after sleeping awkwardly
findings.note: Transient positional symptoms with an obvious trigger and full recovery are benign.

findings.text: Diminished biceps reflex on one side, stable for years
findings.note: A stable, isolated reflex change is a residual finding, not a progressive process.

items.explanation: The discriminators are progression and pattern: progressive deficits and bilateral/UMN signs (both hands, balance, hyperreflexia) escalate; stable, positional, single-dermatome findings stay in MSK land. 'Is it getting worse?' is the most important neurological question you can ask.

items.stem: 78-year-old woman on long-term prednisolone slipped in the bathroom yesterday, landing on her shoulder. Select the features that mandate imaging before any physical examination or treatment.

findings.text: Age 78 with long-term corticosteroid use
findings.note: Osteoporosis risk: age + steroids means low-energy trauma can fracture. Proximal humerus is a classic fragility site.

findings.text: Refuses to move the arm at all, supporting it against her body
findings.note: Complete guarding after trauma is a fracture pattern — do not force an examination.

findings.text: Bruising tracking down the upper arm
findings.note: Ecchymosis migrating distally after trauma suggests bony/vascular injury.

findings.text: She has had mild shoulder stiffness for years
findings.note: Chronic background stiffness is irrelevant to the acute decision.

findings.text: The fall was from standing height
findings.note: In an osteoporotic patient, standing-height falls are EXACTLY how fragility fractures happen — low energy does not mean low risk. The energy of the fall is not reassuring here.

items.explanation: Fragility-risk patient + trauma + guarding + tracking bruise = X-ray first. The instinct to 'just have a quick look at movement' is how proximal humeral fractures get manipulated in clinic. Note the trap: a 'minor' fall is not reassuring when bone quality is the variable.

items.stem: One examination finding best separates these two. Which?
options: Passive external rotation range compared to the other side
Pain severity on a 0–10 scale
Presence of night pain
Tenderness on palpation of the greater tuberosity
items.explanation: Both conditions cause pain, night pain, and difficulty overhead. But RCRSP preserves passive ROM (it's a load-related pain problem), while frozen shoulder destroys passive ER (it's a capsular contracture). Preserved passive ER essentially excludes established frozen shoulder; marked loss makes it (or GH OA) the diagnosis. Pain scores, night pain, and tenderness discriminate nothing.

items.stem: Which single history question best discriminates?
options: Do your symptoms travel below the elbow, into the forearm or hand?
Does it hurt to reach overhead?
Is the pain worse at the end of the day?
Did the pain start gradually?
items.explanation: RCRSP refers to the deltoid region and rarely below the elbow; radicular pain follows dermatomes into the forearm and hand, often with paraesthesia. Overhead pain, gradual onset and end-of-day patterns occur in both. Follow up a 'yes' with neck movement testing and neuro screening.
items.pearl: Below-the-elbow symptoms move your exam to the neck first.

items.stem: Which examination finding best separates a full-thickness tear from a painful but intact cuff?
options: A true lag sign — the arm cannot be held in the test position
Pain on the empty can test
A positive Hawkins-Kennedy
Crepitus with circumduction
items.explanation: Pain-provocation tests (empty can pain, Hawkins) fire in both conditions. What an intact-but-painful cuff can still do is HOLD a position — weakness from pain gives way gradually, while a lag from structural discontinuity drops immediately. Lag signs (ER lag, drop arm, internal rotation lag) are the bedside dividers, with specificity >90%.

items.stem: In a 21-year-old swimmer with shoulder pain, which finding best discriminates?
options: Apprehension (guarding, not just pain) at 90° abduction + external rotation
Painful arc on elevation
Weakness on resisted external rotation
Clicking during freestyle stroke
items.explanation: In young athletes the prior probability already favours instability over cuff pathology. Apprehension — the defensive 'it's going to come out' response — is specific to instability; pain-based findings (painful arc, resisted pain, clicking) overlap heavily between the two. Age flips the pre-test odds: the same painful arc means different things at 21 vs 51.
items.pearl: Under 30: think instability first. Over 40: think cuff first. Priors before tests.

items.conditionB: Bilateral rotator cuff related shoulder pain
items.stem: A 66-year-old has pain in both shoulders. Which question best discriminates?
options: How long does morning stiffness last, and are your hips/thighs stiff too?
Does reaching overhead hurt?
Do you do repetitive work with your arms?
Is one shoulder worse than the other?
items.explanation: Bilateral RCRSP exists (especially in manual workers), so bilaterality alone doesn't decide it. PMR's signature is systemic: morning stiffness >45 minutes, pelvic girdle involvement, constitutional symptoms, raised ESR/CRP, age >50. Overhead pain and asymmetry occur in both. If the answer is 'over an hour, and yes my thighs' — order inflammatory markers.

items.stem: Which finding best localizes the problem to the ACJ rather than the subacromial region?
options: Pain pinpointed on top of the shoulder, worst at end-range elevation and cross-body adduction
Painful arc between 60–120°
Night pain lying on the shoulder
Pain on resisted abduction
items.explanation: ACJ pain is felt ON TOP of the shoulder (patients point with one finger), and provoked at END-range elevation (>170°) and horizontal adduction — versus the 60–120° mid-arc of subacromial pain. Resisted pain and night pain overlap. The one-finger localization is genuinely useful here: the ACJ is superficial and self-reports accurately.
